sentences.text: The largest individuals of Deinosuchus surpassed 9 meters in total length. Despite this massive size, the animal looked similar to modern crocodilians. It possessed a broad, alligator-like snout with a slightly bulbous tip.
Deinosuchus had a proportionally longer skull than modern crocodilians. The back of Deinosuchus was covered with thick hemispherical osteoderms, which are bony plates embedded in the skin.
These osteoderms and connective tissue reinforced Deinosuchus's body to support it out of water.
The first remains of Deinosuchus were discovered in North Carolina in the 1850s. The genus Deinosuchus was first described by Holland in 1909.
A large tooth likely belonging to Deinosuchus was named Polydectes biturgidus by Edward Drinker Cope in 1869. Several fossil osteoderms were discovered at Willow Creek, Montana, in 1903.

Colbert and Bird (1954) speculated Deinosuchus hunted and devoured contemporary dinosaurs. Schwimmer (2002) proposed Deinosuchus fed on dinosaurs based on tooth marks on hadrosaurid vertebrae near Big Bend National Park. Brochu (2003) agreed Deinosuchus probably ate ornithopods occasionally.

Deinosuchus was initially placed in the family Crocodylidae in 1954. A 2025 study by Walter et al. argues that many traits thought to be diagnostic for alligatoroids are actually more widespread. A 2020 study by Cossette and Brochu considered D. rugosus a nomen dubium due to its undiagnostic nature. Cossette and Brochu proposed transferring the type species of Deinosuchus to D. riograndensis.

Deinosuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 82 million years ago. Deinosuchus fossils have been found in 12 U.S. states, including Texas and Montana. Deinosuchus lived on both sides of the Western Interior Seaway, a large inland sea.
A 1999 estimate based on complete remains placed Deinosuchus size between 8 and 10 meters and weight between 2.5 and 5 metric tons.

It is debated whether the western and eastern populations of Deinosuchus represent separate species. It is also debated whether the famous American Museum of Natural History reconstruction accurately represents the skull proportions, as Colbert and Bird may have exaggerated its length and width because the wide snout was unknown at the time.
